title: The Halting Problem
subject: Mathematics of Computing
statement: No algorithm can decide, for every program and input, whether that program eventually halts.
short: A self-referential trick turns any putative halting decider into a contradiction.
long: Turing's 1936 result identifies a concrete question no algorithm can answer in general. The proof assumes a decider H, builds a program that halts exactly when H says it loops, and feeds it its own description. Even a decider that is right 'almost everywhere' fails if correctness is demanded on every input; the obstacle is universality, not a lack of cleverness.
proof: Assume H decides halting. Define D(x): if H(x,x)=1, loop forever; otherwise halt. On input its own description, D halts iff H says it does not — contradiction.
consequence: It sets a hard limit on static analysis and automated verification, and it seeds the entire theory of undecidability.

title: Cantor's Diagonal Argument
subject: Mathematics of Computing
statement: The real numbers cannot be listed: for any purported enumeration, one can construct a real differing from every entry.
short: Change the nth digit of the nth number and you get a number that was not on the list.
long: Cantor's 1891 argument shows that no sequence of reals can exhaust them all, so the infinity of the continuum is strictly larger than that of the naturals. Choosing only the digits 1 and 2 avoids the ambiguity of repeating 9s in decimal expansions. The same diagonal shape resurfaces in Turing's proof and in many lower-bound arguments in complexity theory.
proof: Suppose the reals are listed x_1,x_2,.... Let b_n = 1 if the nth digit of x_n is 2, and b_n = 2 otherwise. Then x = 0.b_1b_2... differs from x_n in digit n, so it was missing.
consequence: It establishes |R| > |N|, founds cardinality theory, and provides the archetype of diagonalisation throughout logic and computer science.

title: The Church–Turing Thesis
subject: Mathematics of Computing
statement: Every effectively computable function on the naturals is computable by a Turing machine, equivalently by lambda calculus or general recursive functions.
short: Very different formal models of algorithm all seem to define the same class of computable functions.
long: The thesis is not a theorem, because its left-hand side is an informal notion: what counts as a mechanical procedure. Its evidence is the convergence of Turing machines, lambda calculus, recursive functions, and later models such as cellular automata and random-access machines. That robustness is why complexity theory can speak about 'all algorithms' without committing to a particular machine model.
proof: One proves equivalences between formal models, each simulating the others; the step from those models to informal effective computability remains a thesis, supported by the failure of every proposed strengthening to exceed Turing power.
consequence: It licenses machine-independent statements of decidability and makes the halting problem a limit of computation itself rather than of one programming language.

title: Turing Completeness
subject: Mathematics of Computing
statement: A system is Turing complete if it can simulate any Turing machine, and can therefore express every computable function.
short: Once a system has storage, branching and unbounded iteration, a tiny set of primitives is enough for any algorithm.
long: Rule 110, the lambda calculus, Conway's Game of Life and many spreadsheet formula languages are Turing complete despite resembling nothing like a computer. Universality is a threshold property: adding just enough conditional control and memory crosses it. It also explains why program analysis for such systems inherits the halting problem's undecidability.
proof: Encode a machine's tape, head position and transition table in the system's state and simulate one transition per step; since a universal Turing machine can run any M, so can the system.
consequence: It identifies which languages can express arbitrary algorithms and which must have undecidable questions about their programs.

title: Rice's Theorem
subject: Mathematics of Computing
statement: Any nontrivial property of the language a Turing machine accepts, one depending only on that language, is undecidable.
short: If a question is about what a program accepts rather than how it is written, no algorithm can settle it for all programs.
long: The halting problem is the special case where the property is 'accepts at least one string'. Rice's theorem says this is no accident: any semantic property with both a yes instance and a no instance is undecidable. Syntactic questions, such as whether a particular instruction appears in the source, may be decidable — they are deliberately outside the theorem's scope.
proof: Assume the empty language lacks the property and pick a language L_0 that has it. Map M to a machine that runs M, then accepts exactly L_0 if M halts and nothing otherwise; the property holds iff M halts. If the empty language has the property, apply the argument to the complement property.
consequence: It rules out fully automatic checking of almost every interesting behavioural property, from totality to program equivalence, and motivates conservative static analysis.

title: The Cook–Levin Theorem
subject: Mathematics of Computing
statement: Boolean satisfiability is NP-complete: every problem in NP reduces to SAT in polynomial time.
short: One Boolean formula can encode the accepting computation of any polynomial-time nondeterministic machine.
long: Cook proved in 1971 that SAT is NP-complete, and Levin independently obtained the same result. The reduction writes a machine's tape, head position and state at each time step as Boolean variables, then adds clauses forcing a valid accepting computation. Because SAT is itself in NP, it becomes the first and most famous universal target for NP reductions.
proof: SAT is in NP by guessing and evaluating an assignment. For L in NP with a p(n)-time checker, build a polynomial-size formula whose variables describe a p(n)-step computation and whose clauses enforce legal transitions and acceptance; it is satisfiable exactly when some witness is accepted.
consequence: It gives a single pivot for the P versus NP question and converts thousands of reasoning and optimisation problems into instances of one formal task.

title: P versus NP
subject: Mathematics of Computing
statement: Open problem: is every problem whose proposed solution can be checked in polynomial time also solvable in polynomial time?
short: It asks whether checking an answer is easier than finding one; no proof in either direction is known.
long: P contains problems solvable quickly, while NP contains problems whose candidate answers can be verified quickly. Since a solver is also a verifier, P is contained in NP, but whether that containment is strict is one of the great open questions of mathematics. A proof that P = NP would reshape cryptography and optimisation; a proof that P ≠ NP would certify a permanent gap between discovery and verification.
proof: Open. What is known: P is contained in NP, and SAT is NP-complete by Cook–Levin, so the whole question is equivalent to asking whether SAT belongs to P.
consequence: It shapes cryptography, algorithm design and our understanding of efficient computation; most researchers expect P ≠ NP, but that is a belief, not a theorem.

title: Boolean Satisfiability
subject: Mathematics of Computing
statement: SAT asks whether a Boolean formula has a truth assignment making it true; it is the canonical NP-complete decision problem.
short: Can all the constraints in a formula of ANDs, ORs and NOTs be satisfied at once?
long: An instance is a formula over variables, and a solution is a choice of true or false for each one. Restrictions matter: 2-SAT is solvable in linear time via implication graphs, while 3-SAT is NP-complete. Modern SAT solvers use clause learning and heuristics to decide formulas with millions of variables, so worst-case theory and everyday performance can look strikingly different.
proof: NP membership follows because an assignment is a polynomial-size certificate checked by evaluating the formula. NP-hardness of 3-SAT is Cook–Levin; 2-SAT is easier because its implication graph reduces the question to reachability.
consequence: It is the standard language for encoding constraints in hardware verification, planning, scheduling and automated reasoning.

title: Shannon's Source Coding Theorem
subject: Mathematics of Computing
statement: For an i.i.d. source of entropy H bits per symbol, lossless block coding can approach H bits per symbol but never beat it.
short: Entropy is the exact price of describing a random source without losing information.
long: Shannon's 1948 theorem gives entropy an operational meaning: it is the limiting compression rate. Frequent symbols get short codewords and rare ones get long codewords; Huffman coding reaches the bound for a single-symbol prefix code up to one bit. Blocking many symbols together drives the overhead per symbol towards zero, but no lossless scheme can go below H on average.
proof: By Kraft–McMillan and Gibbs' inequality, every prefix code has expected length at least H. Choosing lengths ceil(−log₂ p(x)) satisfies Kraft and gives expected length below H + 1; applying this to blocks of n symbols divides the excess by n.
consequence: It justifies lossless compressors from Huffman to arithmetic coding and sets the benchmark against which real codecs are measured.

title: Shannon's Channel Capacity Theorem
subject: Mathematics of Computing
statement: A Gaussian channel of bandwidth B and signal-to-noise ratio S/N carries at most B log₂(1 + S/N) bits per second reliably.
short: Bandwidth and signal-to-noise ratio together set a hard speed limit for reliable communication.
long: Shannon's noisy-channel coding theorem says that below capacity there are error-correcting codes whose error probability tends to zero as block length grows, and above capacity no such code exists. The formula shows that doubling bandwidth helps linearly while improving signal-to-noise ratio helps only logarithmically. Real systems can approach the bound but never cross it, whatever the modulation scheme.
proof: Random coding gives achievability: with codewords chosen independently and typical-set decoding, confusion probability goes to zero for rates below capacity. The converse bounds mutual information by B log₂(1 + S/N), attained by Gaussian inputs.
consequence: It sets the design target for modems, Wi-Fi, deep-space links and storage channels, and explains why error correction works at all.

title: The Fast Fourier Transform
subject: Mathematics of Computing
statement: The discrete Fourier transform can be computed in O(n log n) operations instead of the direct O(n²).
latex: \hat x_k=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}x_j e^{-2\pi i jk/n},\qquad O(n\log n)
short: Reusing shared subcomputations turns a quadratic sum into a near-linear one.
long: The Cooley–Tukey algorithm splits the transform into even and odd indices, recursively transforms the halves, and recombines them with twiddle factors. For n a power of two this costs n log₂ n butterfly operations rather than n² complex multiplications. The FFT is why spectral methods, digital signal processing and much of scientific computing are feasible at scale.
proof: Splitting j into even and odd indices gives X_k = E_k + ω^k O_k and X_{k+n/2} = E_k − ω^k O_k, with ω = e^(−2πi/n). Two half-size transforms plus n combines give T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n), hence T(n) = O(n log n).
consequence: It underpins fast convolution, polynomial multiplication, image processing, spectrum analysis and fast integer multiplication.

title: Strassen's Algorithm
subject: Mathematics of Computing
statement: Two n×n matrices can be multiplied in O(n^{log₂ 7}), about O(n^{2.807}), field operations instead of O(n³).
short: Seven clever combinations replace the eight block products a naive 2×2 split would need.
long: Strassen's 1969 discovery showed that the apparent need for eight recursive multiplications was an artefact of the usual formula. Extra additions buy one fewer multiplication, and recursion compounds that saving into a sub-cubic exponent. Constants and numerical stability make it unattractive for small matrices, but the idea launched the ongoing search for the true matrix multiplication exponent.
proof: Write A and B as 2×2 blocks and form seven products P_i from sums and differences of blocks; the eight entries of AB are obtained from the P_i by additions and subtractions. Recursing gives T(n) = 7T(n/2) + O(n²), so the master theorem yields exponent log₂ 7 < 3.
consequence: It changed the theoretical landscape of linear algebra, helps large exact-arithmetic products, and leaves the optimal exponent an open problem.

title: The Master Theorem for Recurrences
subject: Mathematics of Computing
statement: For T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n) with a ≥ 1 and b > 1, comparing f(n) with n^{log_b a} gives the growth rate.
short: The cost of a recursion tree is dominated by its leaves, its levels, or its root.
long: Unrolling the recurrence produces a tree with a^i subproblems of size n/b^i at level i. If leaf work dominates, the answer is Θ(n^{log_b a}); if top-level work dominates, it is Θ(f(n)); in the balanced case a logarithmic factor appears. Genuine gap cases exist, where substitution or a finer recursion-tree argument is needed.
proof: Level i costs a^i f(n/b^i) and there are log_b n levels. Summing the geometric series: if f grows slower than n^{log_b a − ε} the leaves dominate; if it grows faster by ε the root dominates; if f ~ n^{log_b a} log^k n each level contributes comparably, adding one logarithm.
consequence: It turns divide-and-conquer running times such as merge sort, binary search and Strassen's algorithm into one-line calculations.

title: PageRank and the Dominant Eigenvector
subject: Mathematics of Computing
statement: PageRank scores pages by the stationary distribution of a random surfer, the principal eigenvector of a modified link matrix.
short: A link is a vote, and the long-run visit frequency of a random surfer becomes an importance score.
long: The idea behind Brin and Page's algorithm is to follow outgoing links uniformly, with a small probability of teleporting to a random page. Teleportation makes the transition matrix strictly positive (after handling dangling links), so Perron–Frobenius guarantees a unique stationary distribution and convergence of power iteration. That vector's entries are the PageRank scores, turning a question about graph structure into an eigenvalue computation.
proof: Let P be the row-stochastic link matrix and G = αP + (1−α)11ᵀ/n. For α < 1 the matrix G has strictly positive entries, so Perron–Frobenius gives a unique eigenvector π with eigenvalue 1; iterating v_{t+1} = Gᵀ v_t converges to it.
consequence: It explains why large eigenproblems sit at the heart of web search and why link structure, not just page text, drives ranking.

title: Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems
subject: Mathematics of Computing
statement: Any consistent, effectively axiomatisable theory strong enough for arithmetic is incomplete, and cannot prove its own consistency.
short: Arithmetic contains statements no fixed formal system can prove, and the system cannot certify its own reliability.
long: Gödel encoded statements and proofs as numbers, then built a sentence that says of itself that it is not provable. If the theory is consistent, that sentence is unprovable; with Rosser's refinement, its negation is unprovable too, so the theory is incomplete. The second theorem lands a further blow: a consistent theory meeting the same hypotheses cannot prove its own consistency, ending Hilbert's programme in its original form.
proof: The diagonal lemma gives G_T ↔ ¬Prov_T(⌜G_T⌝); consistency blocks a proof of G_T, and Rosser's variant rules out a proof of its negation under mere consistency. The second theorem comes from formalising inside T the implication that consistency makes G_T unprovable.
consequence: It sets permanent limits on formalisation, underlies results about unprovable combinatorial statements, and reshaped the philosophy of mathematics.

title: The Birthday Attack
subject: Mathematics of Computing
statement: Among N equally likely values, a repeated value appears with probability about one half after only about √(2N) samples.
short: Collisions turn up far sooner than intuition suggests — around the square root of the space size.
long: For a 64-bit hash, finding a specified output takes about 2⁶⁴ attempts, but finding any two colliding inputs takes only about 2³². The reason is that k samples form roughly k²/2 pairs, each with probability 1/N of matching. Cryptographic hash lengths must therefore be chosen with this square-root effect firmly in mind.
proof: The probability that k independent uniform values are all distinct is the product over i of (1 − i/N), approximately e^(−k²/(2N)). Setting this equal to 1/2 gives k ≈ √(2N ln 2).
consequence: It dictates hash-output lengths for collision resistance and explains why a 128-bit hash offers roughly 64 bits of collision security.
